Graham Hughes | Bloomberg | Getty Images Moderna on Friday smashed third-quarter revenue and earnings estimates and hiked its outlook for full-year sales growth, as some of its newer products gain momentum. The biotech company now expects 2026 revenue growth of 15% to 25%, up from its previous guidance of up to 10%. "The new product and the diversification of geography is what has led to such a strong Q3," Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said in an interview ahead of the results. For example, he said the company is seeing the "full-year impact" of its next-generation mRNA Covid vaccine, which won U.S. approval in May 2025. Bancel noted that Covid is a seasonal business and vaccine contracts are typically established in the first quarter, so Moderna's shot only had a "small launch" to start with last year. Moderna's new stand-alone flu shot, which was approved in the U.S. in August, will similarly have a "limited launch" in the country in 2026 given the timing, he said. Here's what Moderna reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 38 cents per share vs. an expected loss of $1.25 Revenue: $1.31 billion vs. $885.1 million expected Moderna shares climbed about 10% in premarket trading Friday. The stock has skyrocketed more than 700% this year, largely on optimism about the potential for the company's personalized cancer vaccine in partnership with Merck . Moderna's third-quarter revenue jumped 29% to $1.31 billion, boosted by higher Covid vaccine sales in international markets and helped by deliveries under long-term government partnerships. Revenue was $780 million in the U.S. and $533 million in international markets. The company posted a net income of $162 million, or 38 cents per share, for the third quarter. That compares with a net loss of $200 million, or a loss of 51 cents per share, reported for the year-ago period. The results come weeks after Moderna and Merck unveiled promising late-stage data on their experimental personalized cancer vaccine in combination with immunotherapy Keytruda in certain melanoma patients. Despite the positive results, investors battered Moderna's stock after part of the data was leaked on social media just days before trial investigators were set to present it at a European medical conference. Bancel called it a "surprising reaction," but said that the companies also saw a positive response from others on Wall Street, including long-term investors and analysts who examined the full data in depth. He added that the doctors in the field "were so impressed with the data," and many expressed that they hope to use it in their day-to-day practice. headlines.article_text: Tech stocks sell-off: SK Hynix, Samsung, SoftBank Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Asian technology stocks tumbled Friday, tracking a sharp sell-off on Wall Street overnight that sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory. Images of mobile devices at the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) Museum of Innovation in Hsinchu, on Tuesday, Jan. 11, 2022. I-Hwa Cheng | Bloomberg | Getty Images Asian technology stocks tumbled Friday, tracking a sharp sell-off on Wall Street overnight that sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory as renewed concerns over artificial intelligence spending rattled investor sentiment. South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged 10.44%, while Samsung Electronics shed 6.35%. LG Innotek and LG Display fell 7.02% and 4.45%, respectively, as selling pressure spread across the country's technology sector. The rout came as investors worried that Democrats' sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to tighter restrictions on data-center development, potentially slowing demand for AI chips and related infrastructure. I n Japan, semiconductor-related stocks also fell, with chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging 4.99%, while Tokyo Electron slid over 5%. Technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 10.83%. Shares of memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings fell 8.72%, while Renesas Electronics declined 5.74%. watch now VIDEO 5:46 05:46 Hyperscalers, healthcare and financials are opportunities in this big sell-off Squawk Box Asia In Taiwan, semiconductor stocks also came under heavy selling pressure, with contract chipmaker TSMC sliding 4.69%. China was also caught in the regional sell-off, with the tech-heavy STAR Market and the ChiNext Artificial Intelligence Index both tumbling more than 4%. The declines followed a brutal session on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5%, amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment boom and returns on massive data-center spending. It closed more than 10% below its recent peak. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged 12.2%. European stocks were broadly lower on Friday, but technology was among the least-impacted sectors, with losses of around 0.25% in morning deals. Chip stocks ASML and ASMI rose 4% and 3%, respectively. The sell-off in Asian equities has been exacerbated by investors unwinding positions, stop-loss selling and heightened volatility, Timothy Moe, chief Asia Pacific equity strategist at Goldman Sachs, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" on Friday. He added that potential political opposition to U.S. data center construction may affect demand and profits for Asian AI hardware suppliers. "If there's concern about the speed and magnitude of buildout in the U.S., then obviously that's going to put all that into question," he said. "The market's tendency is always to shoot first and ask questions later. I think that's exactly what's happening now."
